newsitem.title: USA: Majors seek bigger U.S. emergency oil stockpile.
newsitem.headline: Majors seek bigger U.S. emergency oil stockpile.

text.p: The United States should build up 90 days' worth of oil imports in its emergency stockpile, the American Petroleum Institute said Tuesday.

In comments for an Energy Department study on the future of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, API said at current import rates, the United States needed about 850 million barrels in the reserve, up from today's level of 564 million barrels.

"The API believes that an SPR containing 90 days' supply of oil limports is necessary for the nation to be adequately prepared for possible shortfalls during supply disruptions," the group representing U.S. oil companies said.
"In as much as imports are growing, a 90-day import supply could be considerably higher (than 846 million barrels) by the end of the decade," it said.
Measured against 1996 import levels of more than 9 million barrels per day, the oil reserve currently holds 60 days' worth of oil imports.
To meet the requirement recommended by the oil companies, the government would have to build new storage facilities, because the SPR now has space for only 680 million barrels.

"Although it would take several years to utilize existing capacity once filling is resumed, committing to a timely increase in SPR size to one billion barrels will allow facilities planning and development ot occur in an orderly manner," API said.

The oil companies said the reserve should hold only crude oil, and not refined products as suggested by some lawmakers. Storing only crude oil made more sense, API said, because crude oil was cheaper to buy, store and distribute.
Keeping crude oil in the reserve allowed refiners to pump out whatever product was needed most during a supply shock.
The oil industry came under heavy criticism last year for drawing down its own stocks to cut down on storage costs, and shifting the burden of price spikes to consumers.
To help protect consumers, lawmakers urged the government to build a products reserve, especially for heating oil.

API said there was no need for a government heating oil reserve. "U.S. refiners have demonstrated their ability to cover winters of varying severity with lower inventories," it said, adding that holding larger private or government products stocks "would be unnecessarily costly."
The group backed the Clinton administration's view that the stockpile should not be used as an easy source of cash to balance the budget, and should be used only for emergencies.

It complained about the administration's budget balancing sale last year, which was timed to help ease soaring gasoline prices. "(That sale) can be expected to lead to political pressure on the government to respond wherever and whenever petroleum product prices rise," API said.
